articles.title: "Women reporters will have a harder time": How one NFL scandal weaponized suspicion against women journalists who had nothing to do with it
articles.summary: NFL News: Mike Vrabel is back to coaching football. The New England Patriots are preparing for 2026. And for most people inside the league, the offseason drama .
articles.body: Mike Vrabel is back to coaching football. The New England Patriots are preparing for 2026. And for most people inside the league, the offseason drama surrounding Vrabel and former Athletic reporter Dianna Russini has faded into the background. But for a number of women who cover the NFL for a living, the fallout from that scandal has not gone anywhere. It has quietly reshaped how they do their jobs, who they feel comfortable talking to, and how much extra caution they now need to exercise just to do basic reporting work.Why are NFL women reporters saying source-building has become harder after the Vrabel-Russini scandal?The mechanics of sports journalism are built on access. Reporters need sources. Sources mean informal conversations, coffee meetings, sideline chats, late-night texts after a draft pick. None of that is unusual. It is the job.What has changed, according to multiple women reporters who spoke to ESPN, is that those ordinary interactions now carry a different weight. One assistant coach told a female reporter he would rather not meet her for coffee because he did not want people drawing conclusions about it after everything that happened with Vrabel and Russini. That is not a small thing. That is a gatekeeper closing a door that was already narrow to begin with.Another reporter said NFL personnel reached out to her this spring with a direct warning: "Women reporters will have a harder time at the scouting combine." The combine is one of the most important networking events of the football calendar. Losing ground there is a real professional cost.Four reporters told ESPN they feel they now have to be more deliberate about routine interactions. One said she has started telling her editor when she meets with team personnel, simply because she worries someone might photograph the meeting and it might be misread. These are the calculations that male reporters are not making.What makes it more painful is who was at the center of it. Vrabel had made a visible effort to treat women in the press corps with more respect than many of his peers. He gave the first question at news conferences to veteran female reporters, a habit he brought with him from Tennessee."It really [expletive] sucks that this came from someone who a lot of us thought approached things differently than his peers," one reporter who has covered Vrabel told ESPN. "It's just unfortunate because it felt like he understood there are challenges that women in the business face and was doing one small bit to try and push back on it."That context makes the irony hard to ignore. The one coach many of these reporters considered an ally is now the reason some of them feel more exposed than before.What happened to Dianna Russini and Mike Vrabel, and why did only one of them lose their career?Photos of Vrabel and Russini together at a resort in Sedona, Arizona, surfaced in April. Both said the images were taken out of context. Russini described a group outing. Vrabel called the suggestion of anything improper laughable. Within two weeks, Russini had resigned from The Athletic. Vrabel briefly left the Patriots during the NFL Draft to seek counseling and then came back.The Athletic launched an internal investigation that ran five months. It concluded that Russini's undisclosed relationship with Vrabel violated newsroom standards, though it found little evidence that her coverage was biased. She was still gone. He was still coaching.Vrabel went on to lead New England to the Super Bowl in his first season and enters 2026 with the Patriots circled as contenders again. For him, the story is essentially over.For the women who cover his team and the rest of the league, it is still unfolding in quieter, less visible ways. Every coffee meeting that does not happen, every source who pulls back, every extra email to an editor before a normal conversation with a coach, those are the real costs. They are not dramatic. They do not make headlines. But they compound.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Examining the last 5 Falcons quarterbacks to start Week 1
articles.summary: Who were the last 5 Falcons quarterbacks to start Week 1?
articles.body:
The Atlanta Falcons will enter the 2026 NFL season with a new starting quarterback for the sixth year in a row. Tua Tagovailoa will start in the team's Week 1 game against the Pittsburgh Steelers, which feels like a decision made by default since Michael Penix Jr . has been ruled out.

Switching quarterbacks every year isn't a great strategy for winning games in the NFL, and the fact that the Falcons have won at least seven games in five straight seasons is actually kind of impressive (in a pathetic kind of way).

Starting in 2021, when Falcons president of football Matt Ryan was still the starting QB, here's a look at the last five quarterbacks to start for Atlanta in Week 1.

Passing: 3,968 yards, 20 TD, 12 INT, 90.4 rating

Ryan's final season in Atlanta was not one of his best, but he deserves credit for leading a bad team to seven wins. The Falcons' offensive line was not what it is today, and Ryan was sacked at least 40 times for the fourth year in a row. Atlanta traded Ryan to the Colts after the 2021 NFL season.

Passing: 2,219 yards, 15 TD, 9 INT, 88.1 rating

Mariota was signed as a bridge starter for the Falcons after the team traded Matt Ryan. The former No. 2 overall pick reunited with Arthur Smith but the results were underwhelming. Mariota's season wasn't as bad as people made it out to be, but his viral miscues made it clear he wasn't the long-term answer. Smith benched Mariota in favor of rookie Desmond Ridder, who stated the final four games that season.

Passing: 2,836 yards, 12 TD, 12 INT, 83.4 rating

Ridder was drafted by the Falcons in the third round of the 2022 NFL Draft (ahead of Malik Willis ), and was officially named the starter entering his second season. Ridder struggled with turnovers and reading NFL defenses. His athleticism wasn't the advantage many expected and he was benched for Taylor Heinicke multiple times throughout the season. After the season ended, the Falcons traded Ridder and brought in two new quarterbacks.

Passing: 3,508 yards, 18 TD, 16 INT, 88.6 rating

Cousins signed a four-year, $180 million contract with the Falcons a month before the team drafted Michael Penix Jr. After a hot start by Cousins, he had the worst four-game stretch of his career and lost his job to Penix with three games left in the season. The veteran QB passed for a career-high 16 interceptions in 14 games.

Passing: 1,982 yards, 9 TD, 3 INT, 88.5 rating

Penix tore his ACL against the Panthers in Week 11, but showed a good amount of upside in his nine games. While he struggled with some operational penalties and general inconsistency, Penix put the team in position to win multiple games. The Falcons' kicking woes likely cost Penix at least two wins, but the ACL injury was a devastating blow for the former No. 8 pick.

After a long, confusing quarterback competition, the Falcons named Tagovailoa as their Week 1 starter. The former Dolphins QB was released over the offseason after six seasons in Miami. While the media has treated Tagovailoa like a punching bag based on reports of a bad joint practice performance in Indianapolis, he completes a high percentage of his passes and doesn't turn the ball over a ton. However, Tua will have to play well to keep Penix off of his heels.

The Falcons and Steelers will kick things off at 1 p.m. ET on Sunday in Pittsburgh.

articles.title: NFL execs predict Packers WR Matthew Golden as breakout player of 2026
articles.summary: Who might be the NFL's breakout player in 2026? Execs and scouts believe Packers WR Matthew Golden is a top candidate.
articles.body:
In a poll of NFL executives and scouts from ESPN's Jeremy Fowler , Green Bay Packers receiver Matthew Golden was predicted as the NFL's "breakout player" of the 2026 season.

Golden is entering Year 2 with a starting job intact, more opportunities coming his way and a big chance to emerge as a game-changing player for the Packers.

From one AFC executive: "I'm not really sure why they didn't use him, but I loved him coming out. He can fly."

Other receiving votes for breakout player included Chargers running back Omarion Hampton, Bears tight end Colston Loveland, Buccaneers defensive lineman Calijah Kancey and Giants edge rusher Abdul Carter.

Last season, Golden battled through various minor injuries and a role complicated by a deep receiver room in Green Bay, finishing with 29 catches for 361 yards, and he didn't score his first pro touchdown until the NFC Wild Card Round in Chicago. Gone now are Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks, clearing the path for Golden to be a top contributor for Jordan Love and Matt LaFleur in 2026.

The big question: What would make Golden a true breakout player this season? Going over 1,000 receiving yards or catching 10 or more touchdowns would certainly qualify.

articles.title: How Bill Belichick’s silence on the UNC investigation is raising bigger questions about his control of the Tar Heels
articles.summary: NFL News: Bill Belichick is coaching college football without his defensive coordinator son, without his longtime general manager, and now with outside investig.
articles.body: Bill Belichick is coaching college football without his defensive coordinator son, without his longtime general manager, and now with outside investigators asking whether the people closest to him behaved appropriately inside his own program. When reporters asked him about it Monday, he gave them almost nothing. His son's absence is a medical matter he won't discuss. His conversations with Lombardi are private. His job, he said, is to coach football. That's where it stayed.What is the UNC football investigation about and who is involved?The investigation surfacing around UNC's football program covers more ground than a single allegation. Outside lawyers hired by the university have been asking witnesses whether Steve Belichick used drugs at university facilities or provided substances to at least one player. Those are questions being explored, not confirmed facts. Steve, who serves as defensive coordinator under his father, has been away from the program since early August on what UNC describes as medical leave. There is no confirmed date for his return.Michael Lombardi's exit added another layer. He had joined Belichick at Chapel Hill after years working alongside him in the NFL and in media. Placed on administrative leave in July, he resigned last week. The university said its investigation would continue regardless and that corrective action would follow depending on what the inquiry finds.Investigators reportedly asked witnesses about other matters too -- including an alleged sexual relationship between a recruiting staff member and a player, and possible relationships involving assistant coaches and recruiting personnel. Beyond individual allegations, people interviewed told reporters that investigators asked about the broader culture inside the program and whether questionable behavior had been reported upward to the head coach.That last part matters. It shifts the question from what certain staff members may have done to what Belichick knew or didn't know while leading the program. He addressed that indirectly. "I believe that everybody's responsible, including me, for doing things properly," he said. Whether that satisfies scrutiny depends on what the investigation ultimately surfaces.Is Bill Belichick's UNC program in serious trouble heading into year two?UNC opened this season with a 15-10 win over TCU in Ireland. It was a functional result, achieved without a defensive coordinator or general manager on the sideline. The Tar Heels now prepare for their home opener against East Tennessee State on September 12. Football has continued. The program has not stopped functioning.But the surrounding context is harder to brush aside. Belichick built his operation at Chapel Hill around a small group of trusted people. Two of the most significant are now gone or absent. The investigation has not concluded, and the university has reserved the right to take corrective action. When asked whether leadership had directed changes to how the program runs, Belichick was measured. "We want to run the program in the very best way," he said. "And if there's things we need to do to correct it, then we'll obviously do them."He is clearly trying to separate the football from the investigation. Whether that separation holds depends on how far the inquiry reaches.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
